Field Notes · Nepal, August 2026 · Sep 2, 2026

Flood, Earthquake, Blockade: Nepal's Holy Trinity of Getting F**ked

A glacier let go, a river turned into a weapon, and the one road that ever gave Nepal an out just disappeared under it. Notes on why this isn't a new disaster — it's the same one, with a different delivery method.

Unfiltered Self-Incriminating Mostly True

I've survived an earthquake, a blockade, and a childhood spent tape-rewinding pirated VHS cassettes. I did not think Nepal had another creative way left to kick me in the balls from six thousand miles away. Then Langtang decided to become a waterfall.

Let me back up.

Exhibit A · 2015

The ground that owed somebody money

April 25, 2015. I still remember googling the date years later because trauma doesn't come with a calendar, it just comes. The ground moved like it owed somebody money and was trying to get away from the collection agency. Nine thousand people didn't make it. I did. I don't know what to do with that kind of luck except keep writing about it, apparently.

Exhibit B · August 2026

The mountain that gave up

Now it's August 2026, and instead of the earth shaking, the mountain just gave up and slid into the river. A chunk of Langtang Lirung came apart, dragged a glacier down with it, and turned the Trishuli and Lhende Khola into something biblical. It tore through Rasuwa, buried the Gyirong border crossing under debris, and by the time anyone in Kathmandu understood what was happening, the death toll was already in the hundreds and climbing toward a thousand, with thousands more unaccounted for on both sides of the border. Bodies showed up in India, a hundred and fifty miles downstream — which is a sentence I never thought I'd type about my own country.

Same instability, different delivery method. In 2015 it was the ground under Kathmandu Valley that couldn't hold itself together. In 2026 it's a glacier in the Himalaya that couldn't either.

Here's the thing nobody wants to say out loud: the earthquake and the flood are cousins, not strangers. Both times, the actual disaster was over in minutes. Both times, the real catastrophe was everything that came after — the government finding out in real time, on the news, like the rest of us; the same slow, constipated relief effort; the same photos of army trucks stuck behind landslide debris while people in the actual affected districts are digging with their bare hands. I watched my country rebuild after 2015 at the pace of a man who's been told a broken leg will "probably heal on its own." I'm watching us do the same math again in 2026, except this time the bridge that broke wasn't just a bridge. It was the road to China.hover / tap to declassify

Exhibit C · The Politics

The valve that just got buried

Which brings me to the part of this essay where I get to sound like the guy at family gatherings who ruins dinner by talking politics.

The Gyirong crossing wasn't just some border checkpoint where yak-wool sweaters and pilgrims to Mount Kailash passed through. That was Nepal's one real, physical alternative to India for overland trade. It was the release valve. Small, underused, chronically disrespected by both governments — but it existed, and it meant that when Delhi felt like reminding Kathmandu who controls the taps, Nepal could at least point vaguely northward and say "we have options." Now that crossing is buried under a debris field, and nobody's rebuilding a Himalayan highway anytime soon. Roads like that take years even without a mountain having a nervous breakdown on top of them.

So Nepal just lost leverage it barely had, at the exact geological moment it needed it most.

Exhibit D · 2015–16

The stone age, revisited

I lived through the 2015-16 blockade. I called it the stone age in my own book, because that's what it felt like — no cooking gas, hour-long lines for petrol that ran out before you got to the front, entire families sharing gasoline like it was insulin. Officially it was about the constitution. Unofficially it was Nepal being reminded, very slowly and very specifically, that we are a landlocked country sandwiched between two enormous men having a pissing contest, and we're the grass. That blockade lasted about two months and it broke something in the national psyche that I don't think has ever fully been repaired. We just learned to stop talking about it, the way you stop talking about an ex who still has your Netflix password.

Now imagine that blockade again, except this time the northern door is physically gone. Not politically closed — gone, buried under a hundred kilometers of mud and glacier ice.hover / tap to declassify If Delhi and Kathmandu ever have another falling out — and given Nepali politics, "if" is doing some very generous lifting in that sentence — there is currently no functioning plan B. No slow bleed through Rasuwagadhi to soften the blow. Just India's border, or nothing. I'd like to say I'm being dramatic for the sake of a good essay, but I've already lived the version of this where the fuel runs out and the government's advice is to "be patient" while sitting in an air-conditioned building that has its own diesel generator.

I don't know if there's a lesson in any of this beyond the one I already learned in 2015: Nepal survives disasters beautifully and manages recoveries embarrassingly. The mountains will keep doing what mountains do. The rivers will keep doing what rivers do when a mountain falls into them. And the politicians on both sides of the border will keep doing what they've always done, which is nothing, dressed up as concern.

If you're reading this and you're not from Nepal — I know how insane this sounds. A flood, an earthquake, and a blockade all clustered around the same decade, the same rivers, the same government response time measured in weeks instead of hours. If you are from Nepal, you already knew everything I just said before you finished the first paragraph, and you're probably just here to see if I got the details right.

I did. Unfortunately.
